children.text:
No. It's about connecting two areas/domains of mathematics.

An example would be how you can specify complex numbers in multiple forms:

- as a (real, imaginary) pair using the definitions of operations like addition and multiplication;

- as a 2x2 matrix, with 1 and i having matrix representations;

- as a 2D vector (angle, magnitude).

The idea is that if you prove something in one area you can apply that proof to the other domain using the equivalence mappings without having to prove all of those in the target domain. The basic construction is:

- have the problem in domain A (e.g. a complex number in (re, im) form);

- apply mappings converting domain A to domain B (e.g. representing the complex number as a 2x2 matrix);

- apply the proof from domain B;

- apply mappings converting domain B to domain A;

- QED

In a way, the Langlands program is like a subset of Concept Theory.
Chat is this woo?

The Langlands program is as old as 1967, it translates hard problems in number theory (like primes and polynomials) into problems in geometry and harmonic analysis (like symmetries and waves), where we have other tools to solve them.

The Langlands program just makes sense. The best most succinct definition of the set of real numbers can be put as "a complete ordered field." We usually experience them as decimals and infinitesimals, etc but when you think about them in the context of those three meaningful, powerful words you realize harmonics and geometry make so much sense. And also how primes etc are connected to quantum

The lines between the two are blurred in type theory (which Lean is based upon) where you can express your business logic in the types. Look up “propositions as types”.

Thus the type checker actually does verify the logic of it all.

> if your Rust program compiles then it’s correct” but that never meant your business logic is correct.

These are two completely different things. Lean doesn't check the "business logic." It checks "types."

In layman's terms:

a.foo();

If this compiles, you know that `a` has a type on which `foo()` is callable (type). You don't know what `foo()` does or what it's supposed to do (business logic).

Dumb question but with something like 15 million lines of Lean code, how can we tell when the Lean build “passes” that it is actually formally verifying the right thing and there wasn’t just a “1+1=2” making it pass? Like you hear people say “if your Rust program compiles then it’s correct” but that never  meant your business logic is correct. I’m not suggesting malfeasance or intentional error, just that maybe the model spit out something that “passes” but doesn’t actually prove what it says it does.

It has been extended and specialized many ways since being posed by Riemann over 150 years ago, but perhaps the most important is the generalized Riemann hypothesis which replaces the Riemann zeta function with the Dirichlet L-function. In other words GRH says: All nontrivial zeroes of the Dirichlet L-function L(chi, s) = sum to infinity of chi(n)/n^s, for primitive Dirichlet character chi, have real part 1/2.
